Supply chain diagram for c-Si module assembly 2.3.1 Technology Trends for Crystalline-Silicon Modules The overall trends for c-Si modules have reflected the demand pull for higher-efficiency modules with larger area and higher power ratings, all of which lower balance of system (BOS) costs. Higher module efficiencies have been achieved by switching from full-area aluminum back surface field cells, which dominated the global market up until around 2018, to PERC cells, which led in global market share from 2019 to 2022. TOPCon cells led globally with a 55% market share in 2024, while PERC fell to a 35% share. Manufacturers in the United States have not consistently followed global technology trends. In addition, c-Si cells and modules represent a smaller percentage of the U.S. market than the global average, as the U.S. has lagged global movements toward more efficient technologies. Even while many leading PV manufacturers selling to the U.S. market have switched most of their global production to TOPCon (e.g., 90% of JinkoSolar’s Q4 2024 shipments were TOPCon), PERC continues to hold the largest share of the U.S. market. Section 2.4.1 discusses U.S. lawsuits over TOPCon intellectual property (IP). Monocrystalline module efficiencies have also increased by reducing cell-to-module power losses (by optimizing cell interconnection and soldering) and by adopting larger cells with a squarer shape (vs. older technologies with more dead space on the module due to rounded cell corners). Total module power ratings doubled from 250–300 W in 2014 to 500–600+ W in dc dc 2024 for utility applications through 25% improvement in cell efficiency, up to 40% improvement in module area efficiency through better cell shapes and interconnection, and 50% larger module area (Zuboy et al. 2022, 2023). Larger module area and higher power rating helps reduce utility-scale system costs by reducing the module count and total land area needed to achieve the desired system size (Ardani et al. 2021; Ramasamy et al. 2025).
